items.title: ‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank
items.summary:
Human rights groups report increasing attacks on Palestinian healthcare workers

Yousef Diriyeh and his son Hadi, both paramedics in the occupied West Bank, were lifting a wounded young woman into their ambulance when they heard shots crack and bullets whistle past their heads.

Less than an hour earlier, armed Israeli settlers had attacked the village of Qusra, killing three Palestinians and wounding several more. They were now shooting at the paramedics who had come to help.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Systematic assault’: paramedics blocked and attacked by Israeli settlers and soldiers in West Bank

items.title: Experience: I snapped my thigh in half playing a Thanksgiving party game
items.summary:
Getting over-competitive during a party left me with a broken bone. A family member’s video of the crucial moment went viral and I became ‘the femur guy’

My wife, Diana, and I come from big families, so Thanksgiving means wall-to-wall parties. Last year we spent Thursday with her family, with the weekend earmarked for mine. On the Friday, we’d get together with Diana’s cousins.

We were looking forward to a fun night. When someone announced a game of Eat the Bag (known as the Cereal Box Game in the UK), I was raring to go.

items.title: A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles
items.summary: Researchers have discovered that a naturally occurring molecule released during exercise helps muscles become stronger, resist fatigue, and withstand damage. The molecule, already available as a dietary supplement, could open new avenues for treating muscle deterioration associated with type 2 diabetes.
items.t: A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles

items.title: The religious beliefs of a hospital operator should not determine the healthcare available to Australians | Nisha Khot
items.summary:
Women suffer the consequences when Catholic healthcare providers acquire hospitals and create geographic deserts for abortion, contraception and IVF

In 2012 in Ireland, Dr Savita Halappanavar, who was then 17 weeks pregnant, attended a hospital with back pain. An examination found the pregnancy sac protruding through her womb. Her medical team refused to perform a procedure to end her pregnancy, because in Ireland the law prohibited abortion if a fetal heartbeat was still present. The 31-year-old developed sepsis and subsequently died of a cardiac arrest. During an inquest into her death, a midwife admitted to have said, “We don’t do that [abortion] here. Ireland is a Catholic country.” Halappanavar’s death became a catalyst for the campaign that ultimately led to the legalisation of abortion in Ireland.

This would never happen in Australia in 2026, I hear you say. Except, in Australia, Catholic hospitals provide healthcare based on the same Catholic beliefs as Irish hospitals did in 2012. And this scenario could very easily occur in Australia. In 2022, an ABC journalist interviewed an obstetrician working in an Australian Catholic hospital who described admitting a woman at 17 or 18 weeks whose waters had broken and a fetal heartbeat was still present. As the woman’s condition steadily deteriorated, the doctor was unable to recommend the care she required.
items.t: The religious beliefs of a hospital operator should not determine the healthcare available to Australians | Nisha Khot

items.title: Why aren’t we having more sex? – podcast
items.summary:
A study of sexual trends in Great Britain has found that one in three under-25s have never had sex. So what might be behind the ‘sex recession’?

How many times a month do you think your average Briton has sex?

Do you think that number has gone up or down since the 1990s?

items.title: This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain
items.summary: A naturally derived dietary supplement called urolithin A may help the brain get more oxygen and nutrients when it needs them most. In a randomized clinical trial involving 50 middle-aged adults with obesity, researchers found that taking the supplement daily for four weeks increased blood flow to the brain during a challenging memory task, particularly in a region involved in working memory.
items.t: This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain

items.title: Hospitals in England brace for flu spike with admissions highest for time of year since pre-Covid
items.summary:
NHS chief says hospital bosses should consider asking staff and visitors to wear masks as winter pressures build

Hospitals are bracing for a “horrible spike” in flu in the coming days as winter starts to bite, the head of the NHS in England has said.

Flu and other winter viruses including Covid pose such a threat that hospital bosses should consider telling staff and visitors to wear masks, Jim Mackey said, as figures showed rates of admissions to hospital with flu were at the highest for the time of year since before Covid.

Continue reading...
items.t: Hospitals in England brace for flu spike with admissions highest for time of year since pre-Covid

items.title: Palantir has created bespoke tech solutions for the NHS | Letter
items.summary:
Stephen Childs responds to a letter that said the US software firm was not the right fit for Britain’s health service

Prof Caroline Mitchell is right that US systems designed for an insurance market are rife in the NHS (Letters, 18 November). But Palantir’s software isn’t among them – and should not be confused with a range of other systems, some designed as far back as the 1970s for billing and then exported to the NHS over the following decades.

Our story is different. Each application built on the federated data platform – which connects information across the NHS – is bespoke to the NHS and to the healthcare trust that uses it. The NHS is a highly complex, loose association of healthcare trusts and commissioners, with data that is rich, but often unstructured and frustratingly disconnected.

Continue reading...
items.t: Palantir has created bespoke tech solutions for the NHS | Letter

items.title: Alison Walton-Robson obituary
items.summary:
My friend Alison Walton-Robson, who has died aged 61 of ovarian cancer, was a tireless campaigner for the disability arts movement. Latterly she was the creative director of Headway Arts in Blyth, Northumberland, a pioneering inclusive organisation she co-founded in 1995. Headway offers people from all backgrounds the chance to contribute to the cultural life of their communities and to realise their full creative potential.

The company, which became an Arts Council England national portfolio organisation in 2023, pays particular attention to providing opportunities for artists who are neurodivergent or have a learning disability, and has built an impressive portfolio of projects, including international collaborations. Allie was proud to be an Erasmus+ ambassador and contributed a case study to the European Movement’s successful campaign for the UK to rejoin the EU Erasmus+ education and training programme.

Continue reading...
items.t: Alison Walton-Robson obituary

items.title: Contraceptive pill usage in Great Britain fell drastically in last decade, research finds
items.summary:
Survey published in Lancet reveals ‘hormonal hesitancy’ on the rise – with implants and injections also increasingly spurned

The number of young women using hormonal contraception fell drastically in the past decade, with social media fuelling the “hormonal hesitancy” phenomenon.

New findings from the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4), published in The Lancet, found that almost one in five women in Great Britain at risk of unintended pregnancy were not using effective contraception.

Continue reading...
items.t: Contraceptive pill usage in Great Britain fell drastically in last decade, research finds

items.title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease
items.summary: A combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin produced results comparable to antibiotics when used alongside standard treatment for severe gum disease, with benefits persisting long after supplementation ended. The surprising discovery could offer an alternative for some patients while reducing reliance on antibiotics.
items.t: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease

items.title: Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong
items.summary: Loneliness can be surprisingly deadly, with previous research linking it to a roughly 30% increase in the risk of premature death. However, a new study warns that treating loneliness as a medical condition could distract from its deeper social causes. While healthcare professionals can offer support, lasting solutions may require rebuilding communities and fundamentally changing the way people live and work.
items.t: Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong

items.title: People in the UK: share your experience of private dentistry
items.summary:
The competition regulator has identified ‘a catalogue of concerns’ in the £8bn market. Tell us about finding and paying for dental care.

  • Watchdog calls for shake-up of private dentistry

The UK’s competition watchdog has called for a shake-up of the £8bn private dentistry market, after identifying a “catalogue of concerns” including inflation-busting price rises and signs of targets to sell more expensive treatments and plans.

The Competition and Markets Authority said patients faced substantial differences in prices in different parts of the country and “commercial practices, targets and incentives [that] may not operate in patients’ best interests”.

items.summary:
CMA report highlights inflation-busting annual rises and practices that ‘may not operate in patients’ best interests’

The UK’s competition watchdog has called for a shake-up of the £8bn private dentistry market, after an investigation identified a “catalogue of concerns” including inflation-busting annual rises and evidence of targets to sell more expensive treatments and dental payment plans.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said patients faced substantial differences in prices in different parts of the UK and “commercial practices, targets and incentives [that] may not operate in patients’ best interests”.

items.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar
items.summary:
Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but

When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.

Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its…
items.t: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar

items.title: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
items.summary:
Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice

The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world.

Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously, from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots”
items.t: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams

items.title: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging
items.summary: Researchers have uncovered a kidney protein that may hold an important key to vascular aging and longevity. The protein helps prevent excess phosphate from accumulating in the blood and gradually turning flexible blood vessels rigid. In animal models, a deficiency accelerated blood vessel aging and significantly shortened lifespan, while reducing dietary phosphate helped lessen the damage.
items.t: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging

items.title: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results
items.summary: Robot-assisted knee replacement surgery offers greater surgical precision, but a landmark clinical trial has revealed a surprising limitation. Despite the advanced technology, patients experienced no meaningful improvements in pain, mobility, or recovery compared with conventional surgery after one year.
items.t: World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results

items.title: What the Army's Iowa detonation means for nearby communities
items.summary: The Army blew up a highly volatile lead chemical compound in Iowa after a federal court gave the green light. Officials called the operation a success, but did not take questions from reporters. Surrounding communities remain on alert, and three states say they're monitoring the effects. Stephanie Sy reports, and Lisa Desjardins discusses more with Eliza Billingham of Iowa Public Radio.
items.t: What the Army's Iowa detonation means for nearby communities

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in how the body burns calories
items.summary: Researchers have discovered that a drug can significantly increase the body's energy expenditure without clearly activating calorie-burning brown fat. The unexpected finding reveals a new challenge in developing obesity treatments that harness the body's natural fat-burning machinery.
items.t: Scientists discover a surprising twist in how the body burns calories

items.title: Slashing foreign aid could be disastrous | Letter
items.summary:
Measles is spreading across the world and could give rise to another pandemic, writes Colette McIvor

After reading your report (‘They’re struggling for oxygen’: children pay the price as countries allow measles to surge again, 20 November), I was struck by the statement that proposed cuts to foreign aid from wealthy countries are likely to exacerbate the problem, particularly for those within developing countries.

The UK intends to cut foreign aid spending from 0.5% to 0.3% of national income by the end of 2027. Worryingly, in its 2025-26 report, the Foreign Commonwealth and Development Office proposed a cut of 35% on funding provided to the Democratic Republic of Congo. As your article pointed out, the DRC is already experiencing a deadly Ebola outbreak; with the spread of measles, thousands more will be lost to a different, and largely preventable disease.

Continue reading...
items.t: Slashing foreign aid could be disastrous | Letter

items.title: How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
items.summary:
The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.

(Image credit: Eddie Raynes)
items.t: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia

items.title: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains
items.summary: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders takes potentially harmful medications that can worsen brain function and increase the risk of hospitalization and premature death. Despite encouraging progress over the past decade, researchers warn that medication-related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging.
items.t: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains

items.title: We’re in a flaking epidemic. No wonder no one wants to host gatherings | Chelsea Flagan
items.summary:
We point to self-care as we skip out on activities – but routinely staying home poses its own risk to our mental health

You might have heard by now, but Americans are quite lonely, especially if they’re young.

The kind of low-effort, high-frequency hanging out we used to rely on – dropping by for dinner, meeting up at the park, watching each other’s kids – has all but evaporated from our lives, leaving us unmoored from the social fabric that underpins our most basic wellbeing. (For reference, chronic loneliness has a comparable impact on long-term health to smoking.)

Continue reading...
items.t: We’re in a flaking epidemic. No wonder no one wants to host gatherings | Chelsea Flagan

items.title: ‘The only free thing is a bed’: hospital patients forced to pay as Malawi runs out of medicines
items.summary:
Poor rural families forced to find basic medical supplies as scarcity of foreign exchange paralyses healthcare provision

Two days into her stay at Salima district hospital, Maureen Msukwa is still waiting for a painkiller that the hospital pharmacy cannot provide. In the shade of the acacia trees outside the brick maternity block, dozens of relatives sit on woven mats among plastic buckets, cooking pots and basins of laundry.

Inside, Msukwa, 25, a pregnant mother from Kasache village in central Malawi, clutches a handwritten scrap of paper instructing her to buy paracetamol from a private vendor across the road.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘The only free thing is a bed’: hospital patients forced to pay as Malawi runs out of medicines

items.title: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
items.summary: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.
items.t: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days

items.title: ‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s
items.summary:
Porridge emerges as trend’s poster child with consumers looking to foods that help them feel full for longer, says Waitrose

Sales of filling foods such as porridge oats that mimic the effect of taking weight-loss medication are booming on the back of social media hype billing them as “nature’s Ozempic” or “oatzempic”.

Sales of Waitrose Scottish Oats are up 124% this year, according to the retailer’s annual food and drink report, which dissects the biggest trends sweeping the grocery aisles. A poll conducted for the report revealed that 64% of shoppers are “actively choosing to eat foods like oats that keep us feeling fuller for longer”.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s

items.title: In Waves review – love, grief and surfing at heart of profoundly moving animated tale
items.summary:
Tenderly drawn story combines a history of surfing with an emotional account of losing a partner to bone cancer aged 24

This gently moving and beautifully animated drama is adapted from an award-winning graphic novel by Californian illustrator AJ Dungo. His book combines a history of surfing with a memoir of love and grief; it is an account of his girlfriend Kristen Tuason, who died from bone cancer at just 24. There is something desperately sad in the film’s nostalgic mood: Dungo still in his 20s, already looking in the rearview at his youth like it’s a different universe.

AJ (voiced by Will Sharpe) is a gawky teenager skateboarder who meets fun, outgoing Kirsten (Stephanie Hsu); she’s a surfer and helps AJ to overcome his fear of the ocean. Pretty soon, they’re a couple, hanging out with friends, surfing with a mixtape of sunny bright pop tunes soundtracking their teenage years. Then Kirsten is diagnosed with cancer and undergoes surgery to partially amputate her leg. When the doctors tell her she’s in remission, life goes on. Kirsten trains to be a nurse, while her brother opens a surf shop; another friend starts a craft beer business; AJ is working hard at art school. Life is ahead of them.

Arguably, the film, directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen, is light on detail: characters’ facial expressions are illustrated in simple lines, the finer details of their personalities unsketched. By contrast, the ocean is rendered in spectacular depth and detail, in all its moods. There is a reverence for the…
items.t: In Waves review – love, grief and surfing at heart of profoundly moving animated tale

items.title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
items.summary: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.
items.t: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
items.summary: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.
items.t: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer

items.title: Middle-aged women in England least likely to successfully quit smoking, study finds
items.summary:
Of nearly 8,000 women who tried to stop, only 18% of those aged 45 to 60 managed to give up

Middle-aged women in England are the least likely to successfully give up smoking, according to research.

Smoking is the leading cause of preventable death and illness in the UK. While overall smoking rates in England have declined in recent decades, rates in some regions have increased. About 6.75 million people smoke in England, of whom around 14% are women aged 45-60.

Continue reading...
items.t: Middle-aged women in England least likely to successfully quit smoking, study finds

items.title: England has largest frailty gap out of 31 countries, study finds
items.summary:
People from lowest socioeconomic group in all countries studied had higher frailty scores than those in highest socioeconomic group

England has the largest gap between higher and lower socioeconomic groups when it comes to frailty compared with 30 other countries, a major study has found.

The research, led by academics at King’s College London and published in BMC Medicine, looked at levels of frailty in 71,703 people from 31 countries including England, the US, China, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Greece, Cyprus, Latvia and Lithuania.

Continue reading...
items.t: England has largest frailty gap out of 31 countries, study finds

items.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
items.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.
items.t: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

items.title: Thousands of immigrants with legal status lose Medicaid coverage
items.summary: Hundreds of thousands of immigrants living legally in the U.S. recently lost their Medicaid coverage under a provision of President Trump's signature tax and spending law. The law is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $900 billion over the next decade. Deema Zein reports on what that loss of coverage means for some of those affected.
items.t: Thousands of immigrants with legal status lose Medicaid coverage

items.title: ‘Not about notches on bedpost’: people in Great Britain having less sex – especially young adults
items.summary:
Lancet survey shows under-45s have sex twice a month – down from four times in 1990 – and one in three under-25s have never had intercourse

  • UK adults: tell us why you think younger people are having less sex

Sex among adults in Great Britain has slumped in recent decades, with under-45s having half as many monthly encounters as in 1990 and one in three under-25s reporting that they have never had sexual intercourse.

The fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, or Natsal, found the average adult under 45 now has sex twice a month, continuing a downward trend from four times a month in 1990 and three times a month in 2010.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘Not about notches on bedpost’: people in Great Britain having less sex – especially young adults

items.title: This group of seamstresses mends shirts to make chemo easier for cancer patients
items.summary: Seamstresses in Ohio and other states are making zippered shirts for cancer patients so they can more comfortably undergo chemotherapy treatments.
items.t: This group of seamstresses mends shirts to make chemo easier for cancer patients

items.title: Here's the public health guidance for possible lead exposure in Iowa
items.summary: NPR's Juana Summers talks with Dr. Dan McCabe, medical director of the Iowa Poison Control Center, about how people can protect themselves after the Army detonates degraded lead azide.
items.t: Here's the public health guidance for possible lead exposure in Iowa

items.title: Millions of Americans have medical debt. Experts worry the problem is about to get worse
items.summary: Medical debt is increasingly a risk for people with health insurance, experts say.
items.t: Millions of Americans have medical debt. Experts worry the problem is about to get worse

items.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
items.summary: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe.
items.t: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age

items.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
items.summary: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.
items.t: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat

items.title: Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K
items.summary:
Doctors are fighting an uphill battle against disinformation about routine vitamin K shots given to newborns in the hospital. It helps prevent a rare but devastating bleeding disorder. 

(Image credit: Kate Wells)
items.t: Doctors struggle to save babies after parents refuse vitamin K

items.title: The human cost of the electric vehicle boom is at the center of a lawsuit in Congo
items.summary:
A landmark lawsuit in Congo sees 27 residents accuse a Chinese-owned copper and cobalt mine of poisoning their community and the government of failing to protect them.

(Image credit: Marie Ruwet)
items.t: Bleeding, birth defects: Congo residents sue over alleged mining pollution

items.title: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease
items.summary: Depression in older adults may be more than a mental health concern. Scientists discovered that accumulating tau protein, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, was linked to worsening depressive symptoms in people who still had normal memory and thinking abilities. The faster tau built up in the brain, the faster depressive symptoms increased, suggesting that mood changes could emerge before cognitive decline.
items.t: Depression may be an early warning sign of Alzheimer's disease

items.title: Trump told the Army to pause the detonation of 9,500 pounds of lead azide in Iowa. Here's what to know
items.summary: The U.S. Army's controlled detonation of 68 barrels of unstable lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday is expected to produce a plume of dust containing lead particles that could extend as far as 100 miles away, a plan that residents, lawmakers and environmental groups say was not communicated appropriately.
items.t: Trump told the Army to pause the detonation of 9,500 pounds of lead azide in Iowa. Here's what to know

items.title: 'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?
items.summary:
Several newly elected Democratic U.S. senators campaigned on Medicare for All. Could this be the time it actually gets traction?

(Image credit: Jeff Kowalsky)
items.t: 'Medicare for all' is back on the drawing board. Does it stand a better chance this time?

items.title: More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from Don Toliver concert after an unknown substance sickens fans
items.summary: One person was hospitalized, and more than 50 were assessed for eye and respiratory symptoms.
items.t: More than 12,000 fans were evacuated from Don Toliver concert after an unknown substance sickens fans

items.title: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good
items.summary: Researchers in Japan have developed an innovative gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near-infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria without harming beneficial microbes. Unlike conventional treatments, the approach preserves the mouth's natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells. In mice, it significantly reduced the bone loss associated with periodontitis, a major cause of tooth loss.
items.t: New gum disease treatment kills bad bacteria while sparing the good

items.title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
items.summary: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.
items.t: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

items.title: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis
items.summary: A groundbreaking study reveals that acute myeloid leukemia (AML), an aggressive blood cancer, can begin developing more than 50 years before diagnosis, with the first cancer-driving mutation appearing before age 20 in two-thirds of cases. Scientists discovered that these mutated cells grow in surprisingly predictable patterns, accelerating dramatically as additional mutations accumulate.
items.t: Scientists discover that leukemia can begin developing 50 years before diagnosis

items.title: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?
items.summary: Wellness influencers say mushroom supplements can help with your gut health, focus and immune system. Here is where research suggests there are some links.
items.t: Mushroom supplements promise health benefits. What does the science say?

items.title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
items.summary: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.
items.t: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells

items.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
items.summary: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.
items.t: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
items.summary: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.
items.t: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging

items.title: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds
items.summary: People with type 2 diabetes face a 53% higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, according to a major new review of 40 studies. Researchers estimate that nearly five out of every 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer’s each year. By focusing specifically on these two conditions, the study offers a clearer understanding of a potentially serious connection between metabolic health and brain health.
items.t: Type 2 diabetes linked to 53% higher Alzheimer’s risk, major review finds

items.title: Scientists are fighting for their halted funds. Trust of Black communities may be harder to win back
items.summary: The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer's, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch.

items.title: Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
items.summary:
From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex, a new book of short stories written by kids who are part of the "Read Alex" literacy program in Johannesburg. Participants in weekly classes wrote stories drawing on their own lives.'/> South Africa is working to overcome a children's literacy crisis. In one Johannesburg township, a reading club is instilling a love of books in kids — and inspiring them to become authors.

(Image credit: Madalene Cronje for NPR)
items.t: Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.summary: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.
items.t: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
